nodes.statement: A Diophantine equation is a multivariate polynomial equation over the integers.

nodes.statement: One often considers parametric equations of the type P(a, z_1, ldots, z_nu)=0 where a is called the parameter and z_1, ldots, z_nu are called unknowns.

nodes.statement: A Diophantine set A subset mathbb N is then defined to be any set of parameters such that a in A if and only if there are unknowns z_1, ldots, z_nu in mathbb Z with P(a, z_1, ldots, z_nu) = 0.
nodes.raw_latex: A \emph{Diophantine set} $A \subset {\mathbb N}$ is then defined to be any set of parameters such that $a \in A$ if and only if there are unknowns $z_1, \ldots, z_\nu \in {\mathbb Z}$ with $P(a, z_1, \ldots, z_\nu) = 0$.

nodes.statement: Let (nu, delta)_mathbb N be universal. Then \[ big(11, eta(nu, delta) big)_mathbb Z \] is universal where eta(nu, delta) = 226\,176 \; delta \, (2 delta +1)^nu +2 + 96 \; delta \, (2 delta +1)^nu +1 + 226\,176 \; delta +14\,656. \\ In particular, \[ (11,1.16258cdot 10^63)_mathbb Z and (11, 9.19593 cdot 10^53)_mathbb Z \] are universal over mathbb Z.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:11-universal-pair}
    Let $(\nu, \delta)_{\mathbb N}$ be universal. Then
        \[ \big(11, \eta(\nu, \delta) \big)_{\mathbb Z} \]
    is universal where $\eta(\nu, \delta) = 226\,176 \; \delta \, (2 \delta +1)^{\nu +2} + 96 \; \delta \, (2 \delta +1)^{\nu +1} + 226\,176 \; \delta +14\,656$. \\
    In particular, 
    \[ (11,1.16258\cdot 10^{63})_{\mathbb Z} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (11, 9.19593 \cdot 10^{53})_{\mathbb Z} \]
    are universal over ${\mathbb Z}$.

nodes.statement: The three squares theorem states that for every n in mathbb N there exist integers x, y, z in mathbb Z such that n = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + z.
conclusions: The three squares theorem states that for every n in mathbb N there exist integers x, y, z in mathbb Z such that n = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + z.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{sec:three-squares}
The three squares theorem states that for every $n \in {\mathbb N}$ there exist integers $x, y, z \in {\mathbb Z}$ such that $n = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + z$.
nodes.clean_text: The three squares theorem states that for every n in mathbb N there exist integers x, y, z in mathbb Z such that n = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + z.

nodes.statement: It is a consequence of the classical number theory developed in Nathanson's textbook. Danilkin and Chevalier formalized the three squares theorem as well as its number theory prerequisites in Isabelle. Using this result will constitute the last step in our proof. It serves to ultimately replace the single remaining non-negative integer n geq 0 in Lemma~ below by three true integer unknowns.

Danilkin and Chevalier formalized the three squares theorem as well as its number theory prerequisites in Isabelle~\cite{three-squares-afp}. Using this result will constitute the last step in our proof. It serves to ultimately replace the single remaining non-negative integer $n \geq 0$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:relation-combining} below by three true integer unknowns.

Specifically, M_q can be given as &M_q(A_1,dots,A_q,S,T,R,n)\\ &=prod_varepsilon_1,dots,varepsilon_qin\pm1\^qleft(S^2n + T^2 - S^2(2R-1)left(T^2 + X_q^q +sum_j=1^q varepsilon_j sqrtA_jX_q^j-1right) right) \\ where X_q:=1+sum_j=1^qA_j^2.

nodes.name: Code
nodes.statement: Fix a base B = 2^k for some integer k > 1. Let z_1, ldots, z_nu be given and z_i < B for all i=1, ldots, nu. We say that c is a code for the tuple (z_1, ldots, z_nu) with respect to a tuple (n_1, ldots, n_nu) of strictly increasing numbers if c = sum_i=1^nu z_i B^n_i.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:code}
Fix a base $\mathscr{B} = 2^k$ for some integer $k > 1$. Let $z_1, \ldots, z_
u$ be given and $z_i < \mathscr{B}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, 
u$. We say that $c$ is a code for the tuple $(z_1, \ldots, z_
u)$ with respect to a tuple $(n_1, \ldots, n_
u)$ of strictly increasing numbers if $c = \sum_{i=1}^
u z_i \mathscr{B}^{n_i}$.

nodes.name: Lucas sequence
nodes.statement: A Lucas sequence with parameter Ainmathbb Z is a sequence (x_n)_nin mathbb Z that satisfies the recursive relation x_n+1=Ax_n-x_n-1. Each such sequence is defined uniquely by two initial values, and we define two particular Lucas sequences with initial values psi_0(A)=0, psi_1(A)=1 as well as chi_0(A)=2, chi_1(A)=A.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{thm:11-unknowns}
nodes.statement: By the Three Squares Theorem, any n geq 0 can be represented as n_1^2 + n_2^2 + n_3^2 + n_3. Therefore, tilde Q has a solution whenever n geq 0 and Q has a solution, i.e. when holds. Using crefthm:9-unknowns-ZN, we can thus deduce that P has a solution whenever tilde Q has a solution. The preceding construction uses exactly 11 unknowns, completing the proof of~crefthm:11-unknowns.

nodes.name: Proof of \cref{thm:11-universal-pair}
nodes.statement: Let (nu, delta)_mathbb N be a universal pair. Therefore, every polynomial P can be represented in at most this complexity. Theorem~ establishes that tilde Q always has eleven integer unknowns, independent of P. Calculating the degree of tilde Q now gives the function eta(nu, delta) as claimed. Using the universal pair (32, 12)_mathbb N, one can calculate the explicit value for the degree and obtains that \[ (11, 9.19593 cdot 10^53)_mathbb Z \] is universal.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $(\nu, \delta)_{\mathbb N}$ be a universal pair. Therefore, every polynomial $P$ can be represented in at most this complexity. Theorem~\ref{thm:11-unknowns} establishes that $\tilde Q$ always has eleven integer unknowns, independent of $P$. Calculating the degree of $\tilde Q$ now gives the function $\eta(\nu, \delta)$ as claimed~\cite[Appendix A]{manuscript}. Using the universal pair $(32, 12)_{\mathbb N}$, one can calculate the explicit value for the degree and obtains that 
    \[ (11, 9.19593 \cdot 10^{53})_{\mathbb Z} \]
    is universal.

Using the universal pair (32, 12)_mathbb N, one can calculate the explicit value for the degree and obtains that \[ (11, 9.19593 cdot 10^53)_mathbb Z \] is universal.
